definition: Net Asset Value: the value of one unit, worked out each business day as (investments + cash and receivables − liabilities) ÷ units outstanding.
Assets Under Management: the total market value of the money a fund house, scheme or distributor looks after.
Total Expense Ratio: the yearly cost of running a scheme as a % of its assets, deducted from the NAV daily. A regular plan's TER includes the distributor's commission.
AMFI Registration Number: the distributor's registration with AMFI, renewed periodically.
Employee Unique Identification Number: given to each person who deals with clients and quoted on every transaction they handle.
Know Your Client: identity and address verification required before investing. Status must be validated, not on hold.
Foreign tax residency declarations. Some fund houses restrict US and Canada residents.
A six-level label on every scheme from Low to Very High, showing the risk of the portfolio.
Systematic Investment Plan: a fixed amount invested at regular intervals. Averages the purchase cost over time.
Systematic Transfer Plan: moves money from one scheme to another in instalments, such as from a liquid fund into equity over 6 to 12 months.
Systematic Withdrawal Plan: regular withdrawals from a scheme. Each withdrawal is part principal and part gain.
Annualised return that accounts for the date of each investment. The right measure for a SIP.
Compound Annual Growth Rate: the yearly rate that takes a single lump sum from start to end value. Not for SIPs.
A fee charged on redemption within a set period. It applies per unit, and units are redeemed first-in, first-out (FIFO).
A period during which units cannot be redeemed. In ELSS, each SIP instalment unlocks 3 years after its own date.
The portfolio's previous peak value. A profit share is charged only on gains above it.
The minimum return a PMS must beat before a profit share is charged.
Demat Debit and Pledge Instruction or Power of Attorney: authority a client gives the manager over the demat and bank account. Its scope defines what the manager can do.
Transferring securities in kind, for example funding a PMS with shares you own, or receiving securities back on exit, instead of cash.
SID: scheme document. SAI: statement about the sponsor, trustees and AMC. KIM: short summary given with the application form.
Consolidated Account Statement: one statement of all folios across fund houses, sent monthly if there were transactions, otherwise half-yearly.
New Fund Offer: the first sale of a new scheme's units. A ₹10 NFO is not cheaper than an older fund. It has no track record.
The account number of an investor with a fund house. Holds units, nominee and holding mode.
The time before which an order and funds must arrive to get that day's NAV. Usually 3:00 pm for most schemes.
Portfolio Management Services: a portfolio of securities held in the client's own demat, with a ₹50 lakh minimum and a manager who decides or advises on trades.
Dematerialised account that holds securities electronically. In a PMS it is in the client's own name.
Short-term capital gains: tax on profits from units sold within the short-term holding period. Check current rates.
Long-term capital gains: tax on profits from units sold after the long-term holding period. Check current rates and exemption.
Tax deducted at source: tax withheld before a payment reaches the investor, for example on NRI redemptions.
A plan bought straight from the AMC, with no distributor and a lower TER.
A plan bought through a distributor. Its TER includes trail commission paid by the AMC from the TER.
First In, First Out: the oldest units are sold first, so the holding period (and the LTCG/STCG split) is decided by the oldest purchase unless the fund offers HIFO or FIFO-switch options.
The date a SIP registration is set to stop. It is not the goal date: the SIP can end while the goal is still years away.
A temporary stop to a SIP's instalments, usually up to 3–6 months by scheme, that leaves the registration alive so it resumes on its own.
How a client's money is split across equity, debt, gold and cash, set for the goal's horizon and the client's risk, and reviewed as markets move.
A dynamic-allocation fund that shifts between equity and debt using its own model and risk controls, without the investor having to rebalance.
A pre-agreed corridor around the target mix, such as 5 percentage points either side, that triggers rebalancing; smaller drift is left alone.
The maximum amount a bank mandate authorises per SIP debit. A step-up that raises the instalment above it will be rejected by the bank.
The ceiling on a step-up SIP registration: the instalment rises with each step until it reaches the cap, then stops rising.
A portfolio split: a low-cost, diversified core held for years, with smaller satellite positions around it for themes or opportunities.
How far a portfolio has wandered from its target weights after market moves. Drift is what a rebalance corrects.
The planned shift from equity toward debt as a goal nears, done step by step over the last few years instead of one jump.
Spending that rises along with income, so the corpus a bigger SIP was meant to build gets consumed instead.
How quickly an investment can be turned into cash without a large cost; it decides how much of the emergency fund and near-goal money can stay in equity.
A single fund that holds equity, debt and gold in stated proportions, with the rebalancing done inside the fund.
Selling what has grown past its target and buying what has fallen short, restoring the chosen mix; usually once a year or when a band is breached.
The client's real ability to take risk: horizon, cash flows, income stability and the size of the emergency buffer.
How much of a fall the client can emotionally accept, which is usually lower than their risk capacity.
A SIP registered to raise its instalment by a fixed amount or percentage at set intervals, each year by default.
A fixed long-term target mix, such as 60% equity, 30% debt, 10% gold, set once and rebalanced back to, as opposed to a dynamic or tactical mix.

Income Distribution cum Capital Withdrawal: the option under which a scheme pays out income when declared, instead of adding it to the NAV. IDCW payouts are taxed in the investor's hands at their slab rate.
The scheme option under which income stays invested and adds to the NAV, instead of being paid out.
Planning by life goal — each goal gets its own amount, date, asset mix and monthly SIP — instead of choosing products first.
Trying to buy at market lows and sell at highs. The training material shows it usually costs more than staying invested.
First year's withdrawal as a % of the corpus. ₹4 L a year from ₹1 Cr is a 4% withdrawal rate.
The damage done by poor returns early in the withdrawal phase, when units are sold at low prices to pay expenses.
Splitting the corpus by when the money will be spent: next 1–2 years in safe funds, years 3–7 in stability funds, year 8 onwards in growth funds.
Pre-agreed rules for adjusting withdrawals after good or bad years, such as skipping the inflation increase in a bad year.
The risk of outliving the money.
The agreed share of each asset class in a portfolio.
Checking and rebalancing on a fixed date, such as once a year.
Using new money to top up the underweight asset, without selling anything.
Moving money between schemes of the same fund house. Each switch is a redemption and may carry load and tax.
The share of one fund's portfolio that is also held by another fund, measured by adding the smaller weight of each shared stock.
A fund moving away from its stated style or market-cap focus.
An Alternative Investment Fund investing in early-stage and socially or economically desirable sectors, such as venture capital. Closed-ended, minimum 3-year tenure.

An Alternative Investment Fund for everything not in Category I or III, such as private equity, private credit and real estate. Closed-ended, minimum 3-year tenure; no leverage except for temporary needs.
An Alternative Investment Fund using complex or trading strategies, such as long-short equity. It may use leverage within limits and can be open-ended or closed-ended.
The AIF manager's share of profits above a hurdle, paid in addition to the management fee.
In many Category I & II AIFs, the commitment drawn in stages over months or years, not invested upfront.
Unlisted holdings are valued periodically using estimates, so AIF NAVs can look smoother than they really are. Smooth is not the same as low-risk.
Selling a fund only to selected eligible investors, without public advertising. AIFs may only be sold this way.
Private Placement Memorandum: the AIF document that carries the full fee structure, risks and terms.
The PMS document shared with the client, carrying the fee structure, risks and terms, with key risks explained.
Losses hurt about twice as much as equal gains please, so clients want to stop SIPs after a fall.
Following what everyone else is doing, such as buying a fund because it is popular.
Over-weighting the latest results, such as judging a fund only by last year's return.
Fixating on a reference number like the buy price, such as waiting to sell until the price returns to cost.
Selling winners too early and holding losers too long.
Over-rating one's ability to pick funds or time markets.
Seeking only information that agrees with what one already believes.
Treating money differently by its source, such as calling a bonus 'free money' to take a risk with.
The difference between a fund's return and what the investor actually earns, caused by buying after rallies and selling after falls.
